verdict.text:
Missing-slot detection looks strong on the surface: 54 of 61 genuinely missing slots were flagged, for a micro F1 of 0.90. That number is mostly carried by easy cases, though. Scope is missing in 34 of 35 requirements, and condition in 21. A model that always emits `<MISSING_SCOPE>` would score nearly as well. The slots that test fabrication are actor, modalVerb and action. There the model flagged nothing: 0 of 6 missing slots. The macro F1 of 0.38 reflects this better, but the support behind it is 1, 1 and 4, far too small to support any per-slot claim.

The action slot is where the failure has a visible shape. In all four gold-missing cases (83-Signal, 496-Signal, 1504-Signal, 592-Signal), the model turned the request title into a confident action. "Better identity key synchronization" became "must synchronize the identity keys". "Ability to change maximum size of MMS" became "provide an option to change…". The pattern is consistent: if a title names a feature, few-shot treats it as a stated requirement. As a result, the requirement-level verdict has precision and recall of 0. The model never correctly identified an incomplete requirement, though only five requirements were incomplete. This should be read with care, because the gold labels here are 2–1 majority calls. In 1504-Signal one annotator wrote essentially the LLM's action, and in 83-Signal one annotator filled it too. The model is siding with the minority reading, not inventing something no human would write.

The errors in the other direction are mild and conservative. In three cases (5555, 801 and 175-Signal) the model marked a condition missing that gold considers present, and the humans themselves split on 175. 2055-Signal is the opposite: the model promoted "for each outgoing message" into a scope that gold leaves empty. The output also carries a `<NON_ATOMIC>` tag on a set that was pre-filtered for atomicity. Paska likewise flagged 6457-Signal as non-atomic, and 6457 has the lowest similarity in the run (0.22). These two cases are disagreements with the annotators' atomicity filter, not evidence about non-atomic handling. They are worth a manual look.

Conversion similarity sits at the human-human ceiling. Sequence ratio and Jaccard are about 0.02 below the human-human values, and cosine is about 0.03 above. All three gaps are well inside the roughly 0.22 standard deviation, and the 105 pairs are not independent: there are only 35 requirements, each counted three times. "Indistinguishable from inter-human agreement" is the honest reading. The ceiling is itself inflated, however, by the shared `<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>` prefix that appears in almost every output. The ceiling is also depressed wherever annotators split between filling a slot and tagging it missing. So similarity says little about whether the content is right.

Paska passed 32 of 35. The three failures are one-off smells: non-atomic on 6457, condition order and passive voice on 828, and an imprecise verb on 7310. They show no recurring pattern and are too few to characterise the strategy.

Overall, this run cannot establish whether few-shot fabricates actions, because only four cases test it. The one visible signal points that way and deserves follow-up. The most useful next step is to adjudicate the split gold labels on the action-missing items. Then add few-shot exemplars where a title-only or vague request maps to `<MISSING_ACTION>`, and rerun alongside zsl and cot. Finally, enlarge the pool of underspecified requests so actor and action have meaningful support. None of this should be generalised beyond the atomic subset.
